tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

# wordstat: Interface Contract

## Constraints

- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
- **Package location:** `wordstat/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
- **Entry point:** `python -m wordstat ...` run from repo root.

## Functional requirements

- **R1** `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
- **R2** `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` reads exactly one file, decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`). stdin is never read.
- **R3** Counts, computed on the decoded text:
  - `lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`
  - `words` = number of matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`
  - `chars` = `len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded)
- **R4** `top` lists the `N` most frequent words (same tokens as R3), ordered by count descending, then word ascending. `--top` defaults to 3. Fewer than `N` distinct words lists all of them.
- **R5** Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format.
- **R6** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, no locale use. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.

## Interface contract

### Command

```
python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE
```

- argparse `prog` is `wordstat`.
- `--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error.

### Text format

Exactly four lines, each ending in `\n`:

```
lines: <lines>
words: <words>
chars: <chars>
top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
```

With no words, the last line is `top:` with no trailing space.

### JSON format

One line: the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators, followed by `\n`, where `obj` has keys in this order:

```
{"lines": <int>, "words": <int>, "chars": <int>, "top": [{"word": <str>, "count": <int>}, ...]}
```

### Exit codes and errors

Errors print one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, and leave stdout empty. `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given.

| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| File missing, a directory, or unreadable | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| Usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: ` |

Exit 0 on success, including an empty file. Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors.

## Example

`sample.txt` (UTF-8, `\n` endings):

```
The cat sat.
The cat ran!
A dog.
```

`python -m wordstat sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:

```
lines: 3
words: 8
chars: 33
top: cat=2 the=2 a=1
```

`python -m wordstat --json --top 2 sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:

```
{"lines": 3, "words": 8, "chars": 33, "top": [{"word": "cat", "count": 2}, {"word": "the", "count": 2}]}
```

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	Build `wordstat`, a tiny Python command-line tool that reads one UTF-8 text file and prints its line, word and character counts plus its most frequent words. It must run as `python -m wordstat FILE` from the repository root using only the Python 3.11+ standard library. Output is a short text summary by default or one line of JSON with `--json`; `--top N` sets how many frequent words to show. Output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback. The full interface contract is in `contract.md`; include pytest tests for your implementation.
2

1	# wordstat: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `wordstat/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
7	- **Entry point:** `python -m wordstat ...` run from repo root.
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1** `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
12	- **R2** `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` reads exactly one file, decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`). stdin is never read.
13	- **R3** Counts, computed on the decoded text:
14	  - `lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`
15	  - `words` = number of matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`
16	  - `chars` = `len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded)
17	- **R4** `top` lists the `N` most frequent words (same tokens as R3), ordered by count descending, then word ascending. `--top` defaults to 3. Fewer than `N` distinct words lists all of them.
18	- **R5** Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format.
19	- **R6** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, no locale use. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
20	
21	## Interface contract
22	
23	### Command
24	
25	```
26	python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE
27	```
28	
29	- argparse `prog` is `wordstat`.
30	- `--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error.
31	
32	### Text format
33	
34	Exactly four lines, each ending in `\n`:
35	
36	```
37	lines: <lines>
38	words: <words>
39	chars: <chars>
40	top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
41	```
42	
43	With no words, the last line is `top:` with no trailing space.
44	
45	### JSON format
46	
47	One line: the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators, followed by `\n`, where `obj` has keys in this order:
48	
49	```
50	{"lines": <int>, "words": <int>, "chars": <int>, "top": [{"word": <str>, "count": <int>}, ...]}
51	```
52	
53	### Exit codes and errors
54	
55	Errors print one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, and leave stdout empty. `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given.
56	
57	| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| File missing, a directory, or unreadable | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
60	| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
61	| Usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: ` |
62	
63	Exit 0 on success, including an empty file. Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors.
64	
65	## Example
66	
67	`sample.txt` (UTF-8, `\n` endings):
68	
69	```
70	The cat sat.
71	The cat ran!
72	A dog.
73	```
74	
75	`python -m wordstat sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:
76	
77	```
78	lines: 3
79	words: 8
80	chars: 33
81	top: cat=2 the=2 a=1
82	```
83	
84	`python -m wordstat --json --top 2 sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:
85	
86	```
87	{"lines": 3, "words": 8, "chars": 33, "top": [{"word": "cat", "count": 2}, {"word": "the", "count": 2}]}
88	```

Base directory for this skill: /root/repos/.eval-cfg-20261025T030323Z/plugin/geeky-orchestration/skills/spec-research

Use the shared [workflow terminology](../../AGENTS.md#workflow-terminology).

# Spec Research & Authoring

Deploy a parallel research team to investigate requirements for a new spec, then synthesize findings into a complete feature specification document. The research phase uses 3 subagents with distinct investigation angles to ensure comprehensive coverage before writing begins.

## Arguments

Accept a spec topic or folder path (e.g., `notifications`, `feature-007`, `docs/notifications/`, or a plain description like "real-time notifications system").  
If a stub README already exists in the feature folder (for example `docs/feature-name/README.md`), read it for initial scope constraints.

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Scope Discovery

Before dispatching researchers:

1. Determine the feature folder name. If the argument is already a folder path, use it. Otherwise derive `docs/spec-NNN-<kebab-slug>/`: read `CLAUDE.md` `## Current State` for the current sequence if present. If `CLAUDE.md` is missing, malformed, or the `## Current State` section is absent, continue with fallback naming logic: list existing `docs/spec-*` folders and use the highest number + 1. If no numbered folders exist, follow whatever folder convention prior specs in `docs/` use; if `docs/` is empty, ask the user to confirm the folder name before proceeding.
2. Read any existing stub (`docs/<folder>/README.md`) for scope constraints.
3. Scan the codebase for existing patterns and integration points.
4. Identify 3 distinct research angles based on what the feature needs to cover.

### Phase 2: Define 3 Research Angles

Select 3 non-overlapping research angles based on the feature domain. Each agent investigates a different facet.

Typical per-domain configurations (infrastructure / domain-feature / security-compliance, always anchored by a Codebase Analyst) are in `references/research-angle-menus.md` — load it when picking the angles.

### Phase 3: Dispatch Research Team in Parallel

Deploy all 3 researchers simultaneously.

- **Codebase Analyst**: use `geeky-orchestration:code-explorer` agent type.
- **Web Researchers (2)**: use `general-purpose` agent type with instructions to use `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`.

Each research brief ends with:

```
Produce a structured report with:
- Key findings (numbered, specific)
- Constraints discovered (what the spec MUST respect)
- Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)
- Sources (URLs for web research, file paths for codebase)

DO NOT create or modify any files.
```

### Phase 4: Synthesize into Spec Document

After all 3 researchers report back:

### 2.1 Global constraints (contract.md "Constraints" + brief)

| # | Constraint | Implementation meaning |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | "Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only." | Runtime `wordstat/` package may import nothing outside stdlib. pytest is permitted only as a dev/test dependency, never imported by `wordstat` runtime code. |
| C2 | "Package location: `wordstat/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`)." | A directory named `wordstat/` at repository root. No `src/` nesting. (For `python -m wordstat` it must contain `__main__.py`; `__init__.py` implied for a regular package.) |
| C3 | "Entry point: `python -m wordstat ...` run from repo root." | Must work with the repo root as CWD and no installation step (root CWD is on `sys.path`). No console-script entry point is required or mentioned. |
| C4 | Brief: "Output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux." | Same input file bytes ⇒ same stdout bytes on every OS. Drives R6 and forbids locale/platform-dependent behavior. |
| C5 | Brief: "Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback." | No Python traceback may reach stderr for any bad input; also implies the exit-1 catch-all should print a clean message, not a traceback. |
| C6 | Brief: "include pytest tests for your implementation." | A pytest suite must exist and cover the pinned behaviors. |
| C7 | "stdin is never read" (R2). | Implementation must not open or read `sys.stdin`. A FILE literally named `-` is just a filename, not a stdin shorthand. |

### 2.2 Functional requirements R1–R6 (verbatim constraints and meaning)

**R1** — "`python -m wordstat --help` exits 0."
- Help must be reachable and successful. argparse with `prog="wordstat"` provides this (`--help`/`-h`, usage to stdout, exit 0).

**R2** — "`python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` reads exactly one file, decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`). stdin is never read."
- Exactly one positional FILE; a second positional is a usage error (argparse "unrecognized arguments", exit 2).
- Decoding must use the `utf-8-sig` codec semantics: strip a single leading BOM (`EF BB BF`), then strict-decode the rest as UTF-8.
- The two failure modes of this step map to two distinct error rows (see 2.5).

**R3** — Counts, computed on the decoded text:
- "`lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`" — must use `str.splitlines()` semantics, not `\n`-splitting. Known Python semantics this pins: `"".splitlines()` → 0; a trailing `\n` does not create a phantom empty line (`"a\n"` → 1); `\r\n` and lone `\r` are single boundaries; splitlines also breaks on `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c`, `\x1d`, `\x1e`, `\x85`, `\u2028`, `\u2029`.
- "`words` = number of matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`" — exact algorithm. Token characters are **ASCII** `a–z` and `0–9` only, applied after full Unicode `str.lower()`. Consequences: uppercase ASCII is folded; apostrophes/hyphens/accents split or drop tokens (`don't` → `don`,`t`; `well-known` → `well`,`known`; `café` → `caf`); `abc123` is one token; non-ASCII letters/digits never match directly.
- "`chars` = `len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded)" — Unicode code points, not bytes. BOM exclusion is achieved by `utf-8-sig` stripping the leading BOM before the string exists.

**R4** — "`top` lists the `N` most frequent words (same tokens as R3), ordered by count descending, then word ascending. `--top` defaults to 3. Fewer than `N` distinct words lists all of them."
- Same tokenizer as R3's `words` (so the per-word counts across the full distinct set sum to `words`).
- Sort key is effectively `(-count, word)`; "word ascending" is plain Python string (code-point) comparison — locale-independent.
- Default N = 3 when `--top` absent.
- Output list length = `min(N, number_of_distinct_words)`. No error when N > distinct count.

**R5** — "Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format."
- `--json` is a boolean flag (store_true); default is text format.

**R6** — "Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, no locale use. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding=\"utf-8\", newline=\"\\n\"`."
- Must call something equivalent to `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`. This makes printed `\n` stay `\n` on Windows (no CRLF translation) and forces UTF-8 regardless of console code page.
- "no locale use": do not consult locale for sorting, case folding, or number formatting. Python's `str` comparison and `str.lower()` are already locale-independent — using them as specified satisfies this.

### 2.3 Command shape (contract "Command")

```
python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE
```
- "argparse `prog` is `wordstat`." → `argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="wordstat")`. This makes usage lines read `usage: wordstat ...` and error lines `wordstat: error: ...` — which the usage-error regex depends on.
- "`--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error." → Applies to both non-integer values (`abc`, `2.5`) and integers `< 1` (`0`, `-3`); all must exit 2 in the argparse usage-error style. No upper bound is stated.

### 2.4 Output formats (exact strings)

**Text format** — "Exactly four lines, each ending in `\n`":
```
lines: <lines>
words: <words>
chars: <chars>
top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
```
- Every line, including the last, ends with `\n` (so the byte stream always ends with `\n`).
- Pairs on the top line are separated by single spaces; between `top:` and the first pair there is a single space (`top: cat=2 ...`).
- Load-bearing exception: "With no words, the last line is `top:` with no trailing space." (i.e. exactly `top:\n` — no space after the colon when the pair list is empty.)
- Counts are plain decimal integers (example shows no padding/formatting).

**JSON format** — "One line: the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators, followed by `\n`, where `obj` has keys in this order":
```
{"lines": <int>, "words": <int>, "chars": <int>, "top": [{"word": <str>, "count": <int>}, ...]}
```
- Key order is load-bearing: `lines`, `words`, `chars`, `top`; each top element `{"word", "count"}` in that order. (Python 3.7+ dict insertion order + `json.dumps` preserves it — build dicts in exactly this order.)
- "default separators" means `json.dumps` defaults `(', ', ': ')` when `indent is None` — note the spaces after `,` and `:`; the example line confirms this exactly:
  `{"lines": 3, "words": 8, "chars": 33, "top": [{"word": "cat", "count": 2}, {"word": "the", "count": 2}]}`
  A compact `(',', ':')` rendering would violate the example.
- Exactly one line (the `\n` terminator is the only newline). Empty top is `"top": []`.

### 2.5 Exit codes and errors (contract table, verbatim)

"Errors print one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, and leave stdout empty. `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given."

| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| File missing, a directory, or unreadable | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| Usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: ` |

- Full literal lines for the two file errors: `wordstat: error: <path>: cannot read file` and `wordstat: error: <path>: not valid UTF-8` — both fully specified after the prefix (path interpolated verbatim: relative stays relative, no absolutization, no quoting).
- Usage errors: argparse prints its default usage block to **stderr** and the contract only pins the *last* line to the regex `^wordstat: error: ` plus exit 2. The rest of the message content is intentionally free (argparse's own wording, e.g. `the following arguments are required: FILE`).
- "Exit 0 on success, including an empty file." Empty file ⇒ `lines: 0`, `words: 0`, `chars: 0`, `top:` / `"top": []`.
- "Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors." No specified message format for exit 1; combined with brief's "never a traceback", a catch-all handler printing the prefix to stderr and exiting 1 is the best-supported reading.

### 2.6 Worked example (contract "Example") — verified arithmetic

`sample.txt` (UTF-8, `\n` endings) is exactly `The cat sat.\nThe cat ran!\nA dog.\n`. The stated `chars: 33` confirms the **trailing final newline** is present (13+13+7 = 33 code points). Verified: `lines=3`; tokens `the,cat,sat,the,cat,ran,a,dog` = `words=8`; sorted counts are `cat=2, the=2` (count desc, then `cat` < `the`), then `a=1, dog=1, ran=1, sat=1` → default top-3 is `cat=2 the=2 a=1`; `--top 2` JSON matches the stated line exactly. The example is internally consistent and doubles as a golden test vector.

## 3. Ambiguity Audit

Each item: the competing readings, the reading `contract.md` best supports, severity (High = wrong behavior risk; Medium = test/oracle risk; Low = cosmetic).

1. **What "unreadable" means beyond missing/dir.**
   - Readings: (a) any `OSError` raised while opening/reading the path (PermissionError, ELOOP symlink loop, I/O error, non-regular files that fail to open); (b) only missing + directory.
   - Best supported: (a). The row lists three examples and groups them under one code/message; the natural implementation is "read bytes, catch `OSError` ⇒ cannot read file". A FIFO or device file that opens successfully is an outlier (e.g. `/dev/null` reads as empty → success); blocking FIFOs are unspecified.
   - Severity: Medium (permission tests are also awkward when the suite runs as root, where everything is readable — tests should mock or skip).

2. **Newline translation vs raw bytes — does the input's `\r\n` count as 2 chars or 1?**
   - Readings: (a) read bytes then `.decode("utf-8-sig")` — text preserves `\r` code points, so `"a\r\n"` has `chars=3`; (b) `open(..., encoding="utf-8-sig")` in default text mode (`newline=None`) — universal-newline translation rewrites `\r\n`/`\r` to `\n`, so `"a\r\n"` has `chars=2`.
   - Best supported: (a). R2 says "decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM" and R3 defines `chars = len(text)` as "code points" of that decoded text — translation is a separate, unmentioned transform, and (a) makes the two error classes (OSError vs UnicodeDecodeError) fall out of the read/decode split cleanly. Note `lines` and `words` are identical under both readings (`splitlines` handles `\r\n`/`\r` regardless; the tokenizer never matches `\r`/`\n`); **only `chars` differs**, and only for files containing `\r`. Cross-platform determinism holds under both readings (Python's translation is not platform-dependent).
   - Severity: High (it silently changes `chars` for any CRLF/CR input; the spec must pin one — recommend (a) with an explicit test).

3. **Does the BOM count toward `chars`? / multiple BOMs.**
   - Readings: (a) leading BOM excluded (contract says "BOM excluded" and mandates `utf-8-sig` — one leading BOM stripped); (b) BOM counted.
   - Best supported: (a), explicitly stated. Residual edge: a *second* U+FEFF (`EF BB BF`) later in the file survives decoding and does count in `chars`; a lone-BOM file decodes to `""` (all zero counts).
   - Severity: Low (contract is explicit; the second-BOM edge is worth one test).

4. **`--top` edge values: `0`, negative, non-integer, huge.**
   - Readings: (a) all of `0`, `-N`, `abc`, `2.5` are usage errors (exit 2); N larger than distinct count just lists all; no upper bound. (b) some values accepted.
   - Best supported: (a) — "must be an integer >= 1, else usage error" is unconditional, and "Fewer than N distinct words lists all of them" covers the huge-N case without error. Implementation: a `type=` callable that does `int()` then rejects `< 1` via `ArgumentTypeError`, or post-parse `parser.error` — both yield the required `^wordstat: error: ` last line.
   - Severity: Low (contract clear; tests should still pin `0` and `-1` explicitly since argparse's bare `type=int` would wrongly accept them).

5. **Hyphenated/apostrophe words: one token or two?**
   - Readings: (a) the regex `[a-z0-9]+` splits them — `well-known` → `well`,`known`; `don't` → `don`,`t`; (b) treat as single words.
   - Best supported: (a). The regex is stated exactly and contains no `-` or `'`. Same for accents: `café` → `caf` (the `é` never matches); `naïve` → `na`,`ve`.
   - Severity: Low (contract is precise; the risk is implementers "improving" the tokenizer — tests must freeze the exact regex behavior).

6. **Trailing space / exact bytes of the text format's last line when top is empty.**
   - Readings: (a) `top:` with no trailing space (then `\n`); (b) `top: ` with trailing space.
   - Best supported: (a) — stated verbatim: "the last line is `top:` with no trailing space." All four lines still end with `\n`.
   - Severity: Low (explicit; pin with an empty-file byte-exact test).

7. **JSON escaping and non-ASCII.**
   - Readings: (a) `json.dumps` defaults (`ensure_ascii=True`) — non-ASCII escaped as `\uXXXX`; (b) `ensure_ascii=False`.
   - Best supported: (a) — "the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators" means defaults all round, and moot in practice: every `word` is guaranteed ASCII by `[a-z0-9]+`, keys are ASCII, so the two renderings coincide for all reachable states. `chars`/`lines`/`words` are ints.
   - Severity: Low.

8. **"stdout empty on error" vs argparse printing usage.**
   - Readings: (a) the rule means no *application* output on stdout; argparse's usage/error text goes to stderr (argparse never writes errors to stdout), so stdout is empty anyway; (b) something must suppress argparse's usage block.
   - Best supported: (a). The contract explicitly blesses "argparse default" for usage errors and only constrains the last stderr line. `--help` is not an error and writes usage to stdout with exit 0.
   - Severity: Low (clarifies that no special suppression is needed).

9. **Ordering ties in the top list.**
   - Readings: (a) tie-break by word ascending makes the order total and deterministic — e.g. counts `{the:2, cat:2}` ⇒ `cat` before `the`; (b) insertion/count order arbitrary.
   - Best supported: (a), stated verbatim ("count descending, then word ascending"). Implementation: `sorted(items, key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))` (or sort by count desc with a stable sort pre-sorted by word).
   - Severity: Low (explicit; pin ties in tests).

10. **Which error wins when conditions overlap (e.g. directory vs decode).**
    - Readings: (a) attempt the read first — any `OSError` ⇒ `cannot read file`; only if bytes are obtained does decoding run, and only `UnicodeDecodeError` ⇒ `not valid UTF-8`; (b) other orderings.
    - Best supported: (a). A directory cannot yield bytes, so it can never be "not valid UTF-8"; the read-then-decode pipeline makes the classification total and mutually exclusive.
    - Severity: Medium (defines the required control flow).

11. **Exit 1 message shape.**
    - Readings: (a) catch-all `except Exception` → print `wordstat: error: ...` one line to stderr, exit 1 (satisfies "never a traceback"); (b) let unexpected exceptions crash.
    - Best supported: (a) — brief forbids tracebacks for bad input, and "Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors" implies a controlled path to 1. The exact message is unspecified (only the prefix convention exists).
    - Severity: Medium (spec should define a minimal catch-all without inventing a new contract surface).

12. **`splitlines` Unicode line boundaries.**
    - Readings: (a) `len(text.splitlines())` counts `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c-\x1e`, `\x85`, `\u2028`, `\u2029` as line breaks; (b) only `\n`/`\r`.
    - Best supported: (a) — the formula names `splitlines()` exactly.
    - Severity: Low–Medium (subtle; at least one test should freeze it, e.g. `"a\u2028b"` ⇒ `lines=2`).

13. **Case folding that produces ASCII from non-ASCII.**
    - Readings: (a) faithful `text.lower()` then regex — U+212A KELVIN SIGN lowercases to ASCII `k` and thus matches `[a-z0-9]+` (e.g. `A\u212Ab` lowercases to `akb` → one token); U+0130 dotted capital I lowercases to `i` + U+0307 (combining dot, not in class → `i` matches); (b) ASCII-only lowercasing.
    - Best supported: (a) — R3 names `text.lower()`, which is full Unicode lowering.
    - Severity: Low (exotic input; optional test, but the spec should say the tokenizer is exactly "regex on `str.lower()` output").

14. **stderr encoding for non-ASCII `<path>`.**
    - Readings: (a) contract only mandates reconfiguring **stdout**; stderr keeps platform default, which on Windows may be a legacy code page — printing a non-ASCII path could raise/mangle; (b) also reconfigure stderr to UTF-8 (or use `errors="replace"`).
    - Best supported: the contract literally constrains only stdout, but (b) is the robust reading of the brief's "never a traceback" for weird paths. A spec may implement (b) as a superset without violating anything the contract pins.
    - Severity: Medium (robustness gap on Windows).

15. **`<path>` echoing.**
    - Readings: (a) the raw argv string, exactly as given (relative stays relative, no quotes, no resolving); (b) normalized/absolute path.
    - Best supported: (a) — "exactly as given".
    - Severity: Low (explicit; test with `./relative/name.txt`).

16. **`--top` accepted syntax variants.** `--top=5` and `--top 5` both work under argparse; `int()` accepts `+5`, surrounding whitespace, and underscore forms (`3_000` → 3000). **R3** — Counts, computed on the decoded text:
- "`lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`" — must use `str.splitlines()` semantics, not `\n`-splitting. **R5** — "Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format."

**R5** — "Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format."

8. **"stdout empty on error" vs argparse printing usage.**
   - Readings: (a) the rule means no *application* output on stdout; argparse's usage/error text goes to stderr (argparse never writes errors to stdout), so stdout is empty anyway; (b) something must suppress argparse's usage block.
   - Best supported: (a). The contract explicitly blesses "argparse default" for usage errors and only constrains the last stderr line. `--help` is not an error and writes usage to stdout with exit 0.
   - Severity: Low (clarifies that no special suppression is needed).

9. **Ordering ties in the top list.**
   - Readings: (a) tie-break by word ascending makes the order total and deterministic — e.g. counts `{the:2, cat:2}` ⇒ `cat` before `the`; (b) insertion/count order arbitrary.
   - Best supported: (a), stated verbatim ("count descending, then word ascending"). Implementation: `sorted(items, key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))` (or sort by count desc with a stable sort pre-sorted by word).
   - Severity: Low (explicit; pin ties in tests).

10. **Which error wins when conditions overlap (e.g. directory vs decode).**
    - Readings: (a) attempt the read first — any `OSError` ⇒ `cannot read file`; only if bytes are obtained does decoding run, and only `UnicodeDecodeError` ⇒ `not valid UTF-8`; (b) other orderings.
    - Best supported: (a). A directory cannot yield bytes, so it can never be "not valid UTF-8"; the read-then-decode pipeline makes the classification total and mutually exclusive.
    - Severity: Medium (defines the required control flow).

11. **Exit 1 message shape.**
    - Readings: (a) catch-all `except Exception` → print `wordstat: error: ...` one line to stderr, exit 1 (satisfies "never a traceback"); (b) let unexpected exceptions crash.
    - Best supported: (a) — brief forbids tracebacks for bad input, and "Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors" implies a controlled path to 1. The exact message is unspecified (only the prefix convention exists).
    - Severity: Medium (spec should define a minimal catch-all without inventing a new contract surface).

12. **`splitlines` Unicode line boundaries.**
    - Readings: (a) `len(text.splitlines())` counts `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c-\x1e`, `\x85`, `\u2028`, `\u2029` as line breaks; (b) only `\n`/`\r`.
    - Best supported: (a) — the formula names `splitlines()` exactly.
    - Severity: Low–Medium (subtle; at least one test should freeze it, e.g. `"a\u2028b"` ⇒ `lines=2`).

13. **Case folding that produces ASCII from non-ASCII.**
    - Readings: (a) faithful `text.lower()` then regex — U+212A KELVIN SIGN lowercases to ASCII `k` and thus matches `[a-z0-9]+` (e.g. `A\u212Ab` lowercases to `akb` → one token); U+0130 dotted capital I lowercases to `i` + U+0307 (combining dot, not in class → `i` matches); (b) ASCII-only lowercasing.
    - Best supported: (a) — R3 names `text.lower()`, which is full Unicode lowering.
    - Severity: Low (exotic input; optional test, but the spec should say the tokenizer is exactly "regex on `str.lower()` output").

14. **stderr encoding for non-ASCII `<path>`.**
    - Readings: (a) contract only mandates reconfiguring **stdout**; stderr keeps platform default, which on Windows may be a legacy code page — printing a non-ASCII path could raise/mangle; (b) also reconfigure stderr to UTF-8 (or use `errors="replace"`).
    - Best supported: the contract literally constrains only stdout, but (b) is the robust reading of the brief's "never a traceback" for weird paths. A spec may implement (b) as a superset without violating anything the contract pins.
    - Severity: Medium (robustness gap on Windows).

15. **`<path>` echoing.**
    - Readings: (a) the raw argv string, exactly as given (relative stays relative, no quotes, no resolving); (b) normalized/absolute path.
    - Best supported: (a) — "exactly as given".
    - Severity: Low (explicit; test with `./relative/name.txt`).

16. **`--top` accepted syntax variants.** `--top=5` and `--top 5` both work under argparse; `int()` accepts `+5`, surrounding whitespace, and underscore forms (`3_000` → 3000). Repeated `--top` → last wins. A FILE named like a flag requires `--` separator (standard argparse). None of these are pinned by the contract; all follow automatically from "argparse default".
   - Severity: Low.

17. **Test-suite layout and project metadata.** Contract pins `wordstat/` at root and "pytest for tests only" but says nothing about `tests/` location, `pyproject.toml`, or how pytest is invoked. Conventional choice: `tests/` at root, no runtime packaging metadata required (running from repo root needs none).
   - Severity: Low (free choice; keep runtime importable with zero install).

18. **`.gitignore` completeness.** Only `__pycache__/` is ignored; `.pytest_cache/`, `*.pyc` (covered by `__pycache__/` for normal imports), `.venv/` are not. Not a contract item — a nicety the spec may add, but it must not touch contract requirements.
   - Severity: Low.

Every behavior below is pinned by contract/brief and should have a test:

**Help / invocation**
- [ ] `--help` prints usage and exits 0 (R1); usage text starts from `usage: wordstat` (prog).
- [ ] Runs as `python -m wordstat FILE` from repo root with no install.

**Counting (R3)**
- [ ] Worked example reproduces exactly: `lines: 3 / words: 8 / chars: 33 / top: cat=2 the=2 a=1` (byte-for-byte).

# Research Report: Python CLI Craft for `wordstat`

All behavioral claims below were verified against docs.python.org and, where valuable, empirically on this machine (CPython 3.13.17, pytest 9.1.1) using in-memory simulations — no files were created.

## Key findings

### 1. argparse usage errors and stderr prefixing

1. **The exact error format is `%(prog)s: error: %(message)s\n`**, printed to `sys.stderr` followed by `SystemExit(2)`. Verified empirically with a wordstat-shaped parser (`prog="wordstat"`), every usage error produces a 2-line stderr where the **last line matches the contract regex**:
   ```
   usage: wordstat [-h] [--json] [--top N] FILE
   wordstat: error: the following arguments are required: FILE
   ```
   Verified shapes: missing FILE → `the following arguments are required: FILE`; unknown flag → `unrecognized arguments: --nope`; extra positional → `unrecognized arguments: extra.txt`; bad int → `argument --top: invalid int value: 'abc'`; custom type rejection → `argument --top: must be >= 1, got 0`. In all cases: exit 2, usage line first, `wordstat: error: ` last, **stdout empty**.
2. **No `error()` override is needed.** The contract's "argparse default" requirement is satisfied by construction *provided* `prog="wordstat"` is passed to `ArgumentParser`. Overriding `error()` risks diverging from "argparse default"; don't.
3. **`--top` must be validated with a custom `type` callable** (or post-parse `parser.error()`), because bare `type=int` accepts `0` and negatives. A custom type raising `argparse.ArgumentTypeError` yields the standard `wordstat: error: argument --top: ...` line and exit 2. Note argparse's own int conversion message is `invalid int value: 'abc'` — a custom function using `int(s)` can reproduce it by re-raising with that wording, though the contract only pins the prefix.
4. **`--help` writes help to stdout and exits 0** (verified: `SystemExit(0)`, usage/description text on stdout). Help text is pure ASCII, so it is unaffected by encoding. `parse_args()` never returns after `--help`.
5. Help/usage lines are generated from `prog`, so the same `prog="wordstat"` fixes both usage and error lines.

### 2. `python -m` package layout and the prog-name gotcha

6. **The prog gotcha is real and version-dependent — `prog="wordstat"` is mandatory.** Per the cmdline docs, under `python -m`, `sys.argv[0]` is "the full path to the module file". argparse's default `prog` is `os.path.basename(sys.argv[0])`. Empirically on 3.13: `python -m http.server --bad` → `server.py: error: ...`; `python -m zipapp --bad` → `zipapp.py: error: ...`. For a **package** (`python -m wordstat` executing `wordstat/__main__.py`), default prog is literally **`"__main__.py"`**. Python 3.14 changed the *default* again to "interpreter name followed by `-m` followed by the module name" (docs, argparse "prog" section, Changed in 3.14 note), i.e. `python -m wordstat`. Neither default matches `^wordstat: error: `. The stdlib's own `unittest`/`ast` pin `prog` explicitly for exactly this reason.
7. **Layout:** `wordstat/__init__.py` + `wordstat/__main__.py` at repo root; `python -m wordstat` from repo root puts cwd on `sys.path`. Per the `__main__` docs, `__main__.py` "typically isn't fenced with an `if __name__ == '__main__'` block" and is "kept short and import[s] functions to execute from other modules" (e.g. `from .cli import main`), ending with `raise SystemExit(main())`. Note the docs' warning that `sys.exit()` with a *string* gives exit code 1 — return an int from `main()`, don't pass strings.

### 3. Text decoding — `utf-8-sig`, OSError vs UnicodeDecodeError, and the newline question

8. **`utf-8-sig` semantics** (codecs docs): "On decoding, an optional UTF-8 encoded BOM at the start of the data will be skipped" — strips one BOM if present, no error if absent; BOM-only file decodes to `""` (verified: chars 0). Never use `utf-8-sig` for output — encoding with it *writes* a BOM.
9. **The CRLF/chars question — investigated carefully as requested.** `open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig")` uses the default `newline=None`, which per the `open()`/`io` docs means universal newlines **on every platform**: "Lines in the input can end in `'\n'`, `'\r'`, or `'\r\n'`, and these are translated into `'\n'` before being returned to the caller." Verified via `io.TextIOWrapper(BytesIO(...), encoding="utf-8-sig")` (exact simulation of `open()`): the contract's sample content with `\n` endings → `lines=3, words=8, chars=33`; the **same content with `\r\n` endings → identical `3/8/33`** (CRs consumed); with `newline=''` (no translation) it would be `chars=36`; CR-only endings also collapse (`a\rb\rc` → 3 lines, chars 5). BOM+CRLF file → also `3/8/33`, no U+FEFF in text. **The most contract-faithful read:** "the decoded text" is what a plain `open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig")` text-mode read returns — decode UTF-8, strip optional BOM, translate `\r\n`/`\r` → `\n` — so `chars` on a Windows-created CRLF file equals `chars` on the LF equivalent. This is fully deterministic cross-platform (the translation is not platform-conditional; unlike the *write* side, where `newline=None` means `os.linesep`). The alternative (binary read + decode, keeping `\r\n`) is also deterministic but makes `chars` depend on line-ending style and contradicts the idiomatic "read the file" implementation; it should be explicitly ruled out in the spec.
10. **Exception classes** (exceptions docs): `UnicodeDecodeError → UnicodeError → ValueError` — **not** an `OSError`; catching `OSError` alone will not catch invalid UTF-8, and the two contract messages must come from two separate handlers. `FileNotFoundError`, `IsADirectoryError` (directory), `PermissionError` are all direct `OSError` subclasses → all map to `<path>: cannot read file`.
11. **Decode errors are lazy in text mode.** `open()` succeeds on invalid UTF-8; the `UnicodeDecodeError` is raised when `.read()` (or iteration) decodes the buffered chunk. **The try block must wrap the read, not just the open** — catching only around `open()` will leak a traceback for invalid UTF-8. Wrap `open` + `read` together: `except UnicodeDecodeError` (invalid UTF-8, exit 3) before/above `except OSError` (exit 3); order between them is technically irrelevant (disjoint hierarchies) but both must precede anything broader.
12. `str.splitlines()` quirks that become observable behavior (contract-mandated): a trailing `\n` does **not** create a phantom empty line (`"a\n".splitlines() == ["a"]`); it also splits on a few Unicode separators (U+2028, `\v`, `\f`, …), which can appear in arbitrary UTF-8 input. Accept as-specified.

### 4. stdout reconfiguration

13. **`TextIOWrapper.reconfigure(*, encoding=None, errors=None, newline=None, line_buffering=None, write_through=None)`** (io docs; added 3.7): keyword-only; "This method does an implicit stream flush before setting the new parameters"; "It is not possible to change the encoding or newline if some data has already been read from the stream" (encoding changes after *writes* are fine). `errors` defaults to `'strict'` when only `encoding` is given — fine for UTF-8.
14. **`reconfigure(newline="\n")` matters precisely because of the write-side rule:** on write, `newline=None` (the default on Windows) translates every `'\n'` to `os.linesep` (`\r\n`), while `newline='\n'` or `''` means "no translation takes place". So the contract's `newline="\n"` is what makes `print()`'s trailing newline byte-identical on Windows. If you only ever wrote `\n` with `newline=None` on Windows you'd get `\r\n` — the reconfigure is load-bearing, not decorative.
15. **Call it early in `main()`**, after `parse_args()` (so `--help`/usage errors don't race it — harmless either way since help is ASCII) and before any result output. It also neutralizes `PYTHONIOENCODING`/locale-derived stdout encodings (sys docs: `PYTHONIOENCODING` overrides the encoding at startup — `reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")` overrides it again at runtime). Writing with `encoding="utf-8"` never emits a BOM; a BOM would only appear if the stream encoding were `utf-8-sig`, which the reconfigure rules out.
16. **Under pytest, `reconfigure` is safe in-process:** pytest 9.x's `capsys` installs `_pytest.capture.CaptureIO`, which I verified is a `TextIOWrapper` subclass exposing `reconfigure`. No `hasattr` guard is strictly needed for tests, though it costs nothing. (`TextIOWrapper` has no public `newline` *attribute* to assert on — only `encoding`, `errors`, etc.; don't try to read back the newline setting.)

### 5. Cross-platform determinism pitfalls

17. **`str.lower()` is locale-independent** — it applies Unicode default case conversion regardless of `LC_ALL` (verified identical output under `C` and `C.UTF-8` locales, including the exotic `İ` → `i` + U+0307). Only `locale.*` APIs are locale-sensitive. No `locale.setlocale` anywhere; the regex `[a-z0-9]+` then deterministically matches only ASCII alphanumerics.
18. **Tie-break sorting — the sharpest correctness trap.** "Count descending, then word ascending" must be `sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))`. Verified: for `{'the':2,'cat':2,'a':1,...}` this gives `[('cat',2),('the',2),('a',1),...]`. Two wrong approaches verified: (a) `Counter.most_common()` breaks ties by **first-seen insertion order**, not word order; (b) `sorted(..., key=(count, word), reverse=True)` **reverses the word key too** (`the` before `cat`). Tuple-key with negated count is the correct idiom.
19. Windows console encoding and `PYTHONIOENCODING` are handled by finding 13–15 (reconfigure wins at runtime). Never emit a BOM on stdout (finding 14). Error messages can contain a non-ASCII path (`<path>` is "exactly as given"); on a legacy Windows console cp-encoding, writing such a path to stderr could raise `UnicodeEncodeError` mid-error — see recommendation R4.

### 6. JSON output

20. **`json.dumps(obj)` with defaults matches the contract example byte-for-byte** (verified): separators default to `(', ', ': ')` when `indent is None` (docs: "If None (the default), separators defaults to `(', ', ': ')` if indent is None, and `(',', ': ')` otherwise"), `sort_keys=False`. Key order is dict insertion order (preserved since 3.7): build `{"lines", "words", "chars", "top"}` and each item as `{"word", "count"}` in that order.
21. **`ensure_ascii=True` (default) is correct and desirable here:** "the output is guaranteed to have all incoming non-ASCII and non-printable characters escaped" via `\uXXXX`, producing a **pure-ASCII line** (verified `.isascii() == True`) — which trivially satisfies "UTF-8 output" (ASCII ⊂ UTF-8) and is maximal-determinism. In practice word tokens are `[a-z0-9]+` so already ASCII; keep the default rather than passing `ensure_ascii=False` (which would make output encoding-dependent). Don't pass `separators`, `indent`, or `sort_keys`.
22. The contract requires `json.dumps(obj) + "\n"` — one line including its trailing newline (e.g. `print(json.dumps(obj))` or an explicit `+ "\n"` write).

### 7. Exit codes and error handling structure

23. **Canonical shape:** `main(argv=None) -> int`; `parse_args` handles exit 2 (usage) and exit 0 (`--help`) internally via `SystemExit`; file/decoding failures `return 3` after printing one stderr line; success `return 0`; `__main__.py` does `raise SystemExit(main())`. Exit 1 needs no explicit code — an unexpected exception propagating gives CPython's natural exit 1 (traceback acceptable there per contract; "never a traceback" applies to *bad input* paths).
24. **Keep stdout empty by construction:** do *not* print anything until open+read+count all succeed — compute the full result, then format and print. argparse usage errors already leave stdout empty (verified). This "compute-then-print" ordering is the simplest way to satisfy "stdout EMPTY" for exit-3 errors.
25. Catch `UnicodeDecodeError` and `OSError` as **separate** handlers with the two distinct messages (`<path>: cannot read file` / `<path>: not valid UTF-8`), `{path}` interpolated from the raw argument string (no `os.path` normalization — contract: "exactly as given"). Emit via `print(f"wordstat: error: {msg}", file=sys.stderr)`.

### 8. pytest testing of CLIs

26. **End-to-end tests should use subprocess** (`capsys` docs confirm fd-level `capfd` "allows to also capture output from libraries or subprocesses"; for a full `python -m` invocation, plain `subprocess.run` is the tool): `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "wordstat", str(f)], cwd=repo_root, capture_output=True)` — assert `result.returncode` and **compare `result.stdout`/`result.stderr` as bytes** (`== b"lines: 3\nwords: 8\n..."`). Bytes comparison avoids Python's own text-mode universal-newline reading in subprocess masking a Windows `\r\n` bug, and `sys.executable` guarantees the same interpreter.
